item.text: {"additional_concerns":["The marketing claim's reference to missing paragraphs is stale: the supplied source includes the services context and surrounding marketing provisions. Both extracted claims are supported, but neither answers the selected gift questions.","node.2a6321b4ce90763bf0be564e places offering in scope. node.6d6e7adc6faa9d94b74c08e5, node.968dbccb08282a4e8a580ae5, node.97af37a2579f59b0ee43211f and node.bca408c75cbf8467afafada6 place promotional linkage in scope. Known absence therefore yields OUT_OF_SCOPE rather than the typed question's negative prohibition answer or positive gift-compliance answer. Whether this is intentional domain restriction or a correspondence defect remains unresolved.","The two offer-level candidates combine an offer-level promotional link with existence of a non-discount gift. They do not explicitly require that the same gift component has the promotional link. Mixed offers could therefore produce an unsupported prohibition unless the supplied classifications establish that connection.","node.142f34016b300f5c110eb249 uses 'provider' for the regulated actor. It must denote the distributor offering the component; treating funding or fulfilment as a prerequisite would add a restriction not stated in the circular.","The circular's definition of distributors supports the SFC-authorised-fund context. Paragraph 3.11 is quoted in broader investment-product terms; application beyond the circular's context is not established by this review.","External Code of Conduct paragraphs 3.11 and 2.3, SFO section 103, and the answer to question 1 of the SFC FAQ issued on 30 September 2010 are absent. No supplied dependency IDs identify them. They are unnecessary to establish these two express circular claims, but are needed for independent interpretation of the full standards, statutory exemptions or disputed gift classifications.","The supplied text establishes no concrete effective interval. The candidates' generic temporal descriptions do not establish historical or current applicability.","Gift classification and exception classification remain supplied judgments. The source says incentives 'may be considered a gift'; neither incentive status nor a guaranteed return alone establishes prohibition.
